decks.title: Oxidation and Reduction — Part 1: Oxygen, hydrogen and electrons
goals: Identify the substance oxidised and the substance reduced using oxygen and hydrogen transfer
Define oxidation and reduction as loss and gain of electrons
Write ionic half-changes showing loss and gain of electrons

slides.heading: Two changes that never travel alone
slides.body_md: Part 1 — burning, and the change of a metal oxide into a metal, look like opposites. Chemists call them **oxidation** and **reduction**, and they always happen together.

visual.alt: Flow: one substance is oxidised while another is reduced

slides.narration: Burning a metal in air is one kind of chemical change. Turning a metal oxide back into the metal is another. They look like opposites. Chemists call them oxidation and reduction, and one of them can never happen without the other.

slides.heading: Oxygen: added or removed
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** is the addition of oxygen. **Reduction** is the removal of oxygen.

visual.alt: Table of four changes classified by oxygen added or removed

slides.narration: The first way to look at it is through oxygen. Adding oxygen to a substance is oxidation, so magnesium becoming magnesium oxide is oxidation. Removing oxygen is reduction, so lead oxide becoming lead is reduction.

slides.heading: Hydrogen: removed or added
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** is the removal of hydrogen. **Reduction** is the addition of hydrogen.

visual.alt: Table of four changes classified by hydrogen removed or added

slides.narration: The second way uses hydrogen, and it works the other way round. Taking hydrogen away from a substance is oxidation. Adding hydrogen to a substance is reduction. So hydrogen sulphide changing into sulphur is oxidation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: lead oxide and hydrogen
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Dry hydrogen is passed over heated yellow lead(II) oxide, $\ce{PbO + H2 -> Pb + H2O}$. Which substance is oxidised and which is reduced?

**Step 1.** Lead(II) oxide **loses oxygen** and becomes lead, so it is **reduced**.

**Step 2.** Hydrogen **gains oxygen** and becomes water, so it is **oxidised**.

**Step 3.** Both happen in the same reaction.

visual.alt: Lead oxide and hydrogen give lead and water
visual.caption: Lead oxide is reduced; hydrogen is oxidised.

slides.narration: Look at what happens to oxygen. Lead oxide loses its oxygen and turns into grey lead, so lead oxide is reduced. The same oxygen goes to hydrogen, which becomes water, so hydrogen is oxidised. One substance is reduced and the other is oxidised in the same reaction.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxygen transfer
slides.body_md: Follow the oxygen.

visual.alt: Magnesium and carbon dioxide give magnesium oxide and carbon

slides.narration: Magnesium burns in carbon dioxide and leaves white magnesium oxide and black carbon. Which statement is correct?

slides.heading: A single reaction shows both
slides.body_md: Whenever one substance **gains oxygen**, another substance **loses** that oxygen.

visual.alt: Flow: lead oxide gives oxygen to hydrogen

slides.narration: Oxygen cannot just vanish. If one substance gains oxygen, another substance must give it up. So oxidation of one substance always comes with reduction of another. That pair of changes is called a redox reaction.

slides.heading: The electronic concept
slides.body_md: **Oxidation** is the **loss** of electrons. **Reduction** is the **gain** of electrons.

slides.narration: A sodium atom has one electron in its outer shell. It loses that electron and becomes a sodium ion, which is oxidation. A chlorine atom has seven outer electrons. It gains the electron and becomes a chloride ion, which is reduction. The electron lost by one is gained by the other.

slides.heading: Writing half-changes
slides.body_md: Each change is written separately as a **half-change**, with electrons shown. Both **atoms** and **charge** must balance.

visual.alt: Table of four oxidation half-changes and four reduction half-changes

slides.narration: A half-change shows only one of the two changes. In an oxidation, the electrons appear on the right side. In a reduction, the electrons appear on the left side. Check that atoms and also electric charge balance on both sides.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: balancing a half-change
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Write the half-change for the reduction of a chlorine molecule to chloride ions.

**Step 1.** Start with $\ce{Cl2 -> 2Cl-}$: the atoms balance, but the charge does not (0 on the left, −2 on the right).

**Step 2.** Add electrons to the **left** to make the charges equal: $\ce{Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-}$.

**Step 3.** Two electrons are gained, so chlorine is **reduced**.

visual.alt: A chlorine molecule gains two electrons and gives two chloride ions
visual.caption: Charge: 2 × (−1) = −2 on both sides.

slides.narration: Start with the atoms. One chlorine molecule gives two chloride ions, so the atoms balance. But the charge is zero on the left and minus two on the right. Add two electrons to the left. Now both sides have a charge of minus two. Electrons are gained, so this is reduction.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a half-change
slides.body_md: Where are the electrons?

visual.alt: A copper ion gains two electrons to form copper

slides.narration: A copper two plus ion gains two electrons and becomes a copper atom. Which statement describes this change?

slides.heading: Joining two half-changes
slides.body_md: The **electrons lost** must equal the **electrons gained**. Add the halves so the electrons cancel: $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$ and $\ce{Fe^2+ + 2e- -> Fe}$.

visual.alt: Magnesium and iron(II) ions give magnesium ions and iron
visual.caption: Electrons exchanged: 2; they cancel and are not written.

slides.narration: Here the oxidation gives away two electrons and the reduction takes two electrons. They are equal, so they cancel. The result is magnesium plus iron two plus ions giving magnesium two plus ions and iron. No electrons are left in the final equation.

slides.heading: When the electrons are not equal
slides.body_md: If the numbers differ, **multiply** each half so they match. Aluminium loses 3; the iron(II) ion gains 2, so use **2 Al** and **3 Fe²⁺**, giving 6 electrons each way.

visual.alt: Table showing how two half-changes are multiplied and added

slides.narration: Sometimes the numbers of electrons are different. Aluminium gives three electrons, and an iron two plus ion takes two. The smallest number that both divide into is six. So we use two aluminium atoms and three iron ions. Six electrons are lost and six are gained.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidation or reduction?
slides.body_md: Compare the charge on the iron before and after.

visual.alt: An iron(II) ion loses an electron and becomes an iron(III) ion

slides.narration: An iron two plus ion changes into an iron three plus ion. Which of the following half-changes shows an oxidation?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Oxidation: addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, loss of electrons.
Reduction: removal of oxygen, addition of hydrogen, gain of electrons.
Oxidation and reduction always occur together in a redox reaction.
Half-changes show the electrons; atoms and charge must both balance, and the electrons must cancel when two halves are added.

visual.alt: Summary table of oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen, hydrogen and electrons

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Oxidation is gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen or loss of electrons. Reduction is the opposite in every case. They always occur together. Half-changes show the electrons, and when two halves are added the electrons must cancel.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Put the electrons on the right for oxidation and on the left for reduction.
Check the charge as well as the atoms in a half-change.
Write ions with their charge: Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cl⁻.
Always name both the substance oxidised and the substance reduced.

rows: Writing Na → Na⁺ with no electron
Saying oxidation is gain of electrons
Leaving electrons in the final equation
They cancel when halves are added

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips. Write electrons on the right for oxidation and on the left for reduction. Balance charge as well as atoms. Write each ion with its charge. And name both the substance oxidised and the substance reduced.

decks.title: Oxidation and Reduction — Part 2: Oxidising agents, reducing agents and redox reactions
goals: Identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in a redox reaction
Recognise redox reactions and reactions that are not redox
Use colour changes and electron transfer to describe a redox reaction

slides.heading: Who does the work?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — a substance that is oxidised needs a partner that takes something from it. That partner is the **oxidising agent**.

visual.alt: Flow: the reducing agent gives electrons to the oxidising agent

slides.narration: In a redox reaction each substance has a job. One substance does the oxidising and is itself reduced. The other does the reducing and is itself oxidised. This part is about naming these agents correctly.

slides.heading: Oxidising agent
slides.body_md: An **oxidising agent** causes oxidation in another substance, and is itself **reduced**.

visual.alt: Table of three descriptions of an oxidising agent

slides.narration: An oxidising agent oxidises another substance. It may give oxygen, take away hydrogen, or take electrons. In every case the oxidising agent is itself reduced. It gains electrons.

slides.heading: Reducing agent
slides.body_md: A **reducing agent** causes reduction in another substance, and is itself **oxidised**.

visual.alt: Table of three descriptions of a reducing agent

slides.narration: A reducing agent reduces another substance. It may take away oxygen, give hydrogen, or give electrons. It is always oxidised itself. It loses electrons.

slides.heading: Common agents

rows: Reactive metals such as sodium, magnesium and zinc

visual.alt: Table of five common oxidising agents and five common reducing agents

slides.narration: Here are some common agents. Oxygen, chlorine and nitric acid are oxidising agents. So are hydrogen peroxide and potassium permanganate. Hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide and reactive metals are reducing agents. Metals are good reducing agents because they lose electrons easily.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: chlorine and hydrogen sulphide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Chlorine gas is passed into a solution of hydrogen sulphide, $\ce{Cl2 + H2S -> 2HCl + S}$, and a yellow solid forms. Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent.

**Step 1.** $\ce{H2S}$ **loses hydrogen** and becomes sulphur: it is **oxidised**, so it is the **reducing agent**.

**Step 2.** $\ce{Cl2}$ **gains hydrogen** and becomes hydrogen chloride: it is **reduced**, so it is the **oxidising agent**.

**Step 3.** The yellow solid is sulphur.

visual.alt: Chlorine and hydrogen sulphide give hydrogen chloride and sulphur
visual.caption: Chlorine: oxidising agent. Hydrogen sulphide: reducing agent.

slides.narration: Look at the hydrogen. Hydrogen sulphide loses hydrogen and becomes yellow sulphur, so it is oxidised and is the reducing agent. Chlorine gains hydrogen to form hydrogen chloride, so it is reduced and is the oxidising agent.

slides.heading: Quick check: agents
slides.body_md: The agent is the substance that does the changing, not the one that changes.

visual.alt: Zinc and copper oxide give zinc oxide and copper

slides.narration: Zinc powder is heated with black copper oxide, and reddish brown copper is formed. Which substance is the reducing agent?

slides.heading: Electron view: magnesium in copper sulphate
slides.body_md: Magnesium is the **reducing agent** (it loses electrons); the copper(II) ion is the **oxidising agent** (it gains them). Together: $\ce{Mg + Cu^2+ -> Mg^2+ + Cu}$.

Copper ions gain those electrons and settle as reddish brown copper. Magnesium is the reducing agent and the copper ion is the oxidising agent.

slides.body_md: Which of the two reactants gains the electrons?

slides.heading: Spotting a redox reaction

rows: Magnesium burning; lead oxide changing to lead
A metal going into solution as ions, or ions turning into a metal
A colour change that goes with these
Pale green iron(II) to yellow iron(III); brown iodine from iodide

visual.alt: Table of clues that a reaction is a redox reaction

slides.narration: How can you spot a redox reaction? Look for oxygen or hydrogen being gained or lost. Look for a metal changing into ions or ions changing into a metal. And watch for colour changes, such as pale green iron two solution turning yellow, or brown iodine appearing.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: chlorine and iron(II) chloride
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Chlorine is passed into pale green iron(II) chloride solution, which turns yellow: $\ce{2FeCl2 + Cl2 -> 2FeCl3}$. Write the half-changes and name the agents.

**Step 1.** Oxidation: $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ (the electron is lost).

**Step 2.** Reduction: $\ce{Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-}$.

**Step 3.** Use 2 Fe²⁺ for each Cl₂ so that 2 electrons are lost and 2 gained. Iron(II) is the reducing agent; chlorine is the oxidising agent.

visual.alt: Iron(II) ions and chlorine give iron(III) ions and chloride ions
visual.caption: Charge: +4 on the left; +6 − 2 = +4 on the right.

slides.narration: Iron two plus loses one electron to become iron three plus, which is oxidation. Chlorine gains two electrons, which is reduction. Because chlorine needs two electrons, two iron ions are used for each chlorine molecule. Iron two is the reducing agent, and chlorine is the oxidising agent.

slides.heading: Quick check: is it redox?
slides.body_md: Look for a gain or loss of electrons, oxygen or hydrogen.

visual.alt: Two reactions and their types

slides.narration: Four reactions are listed. Which one is a redox reaction?

slides.heading: Not every reaction is redox
slides.body_md: A precipitation or a neutralisation involves **no loss or gain of electrons**. Only the partners are exchanged.

rows: No electron or oxygen transfer to another substance
Sodium loses and chlorine gains electrons

visual.alt: Table of four reactions and whether each is redox

slides.narration: Not every reaction is a redox reaction. When silver nitrate and sodium chloride react, the ions only swap partners and no electrons move. The same is true for neutralisation. In a redox reaction, electrons, oxygen or hydrogen are transferred.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Oxidising agent: causes oxidation, is reduced, gains electrons.
Reducing agent: causes reduction, is oxidised, loses electrons.
Redox reaction: oxidation and reduction together; check what each reactant gains or loses.
Precipitation and neutralisation are not redox reactions.

visual.alt: Summary table of oxidising and reducing agents

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. An oxidising agent is itself reduced and gains electrons. A reducing agent is itself oxidised and loses electrons. A redox reaction has both. Precipitation and neutralisation are not redox reactions.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: The agent is the substance that is oxidised or reduced by the other: the reducing agent is the one oxidised.
Give a reason in terms of oxygen, hydrogen or electrons.
Name the colour changes you see, such as pale green to yellow.
Write half-changes with the electrons on the correct side.

rows: Calling the substance reduced the reducing agent
The reducing agent is the one oxidised
Calling a precipitation a redox reaction

slides.narration: Exam tips. The reducing agent is the substance that is itself oxidised. Always give a reason in terms of oxygen, hydrogen or electrons. Describe the colour changes. And write half-changes with electrons on the right side.

notes.title: Oxidation and Reduction — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Oxidation and reduction: oxygen and hydrogen
sections.body_md:
The first idea of oxidation and reduction is about the transfer of oxygen and hydrogen.

| | Oxidation | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | **Addition** of oxygen | **Removal** of oxygen |
| Hydrogen | **Removal** of hydrogen | **Addition** of hydrogen |

| Reaction | Oxidised | Reduced |
|---|---|---|
| $\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}$ | Magnesium (gains oxygen) | Oxygen (it gains electrons; see section 2) |
| $\ce{PbO + H2 -> Pb + H2O}$ | Hydrogen (gains oxygen) | Lead(II) oxide (loses oxygen) |
| $\ce{2Mg + CO2 -> 2MgO + C}$ | Magnesium (gains oxygen) | Carbon dioxide (loses oxygen) |
| $\ce{2CO + O2 -> 2CO2}$ | Carbon monoxide (gains oxygen) | Oxygen (it gains electrons; see section 2) |
| $\ce{Cl2 + H2S -> 2HCl + S}$ | Hydrogen sulphide (loses hydrogen) | Chlorine (gains hydrogen) |
| $\ce{MnO2 + 4HCl -> MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2}$ | Hydrochloric acid (loses hydrogen) | Manganese(IV) oxide (loses oxygen) |

**Oxidation and reduction occur together.** When one substance gains oxygen, another loses it; when one loses hydrogen, another gains it. A reaction in which both take place is a **redox reaction**.

key_terms.definition_md: Addition of oxygen to a substance, or removal of hydrogen from it (and loss of electrons).
Removal of oxygen from a substance, or addition of hydrogen to it (and gain of electrons).
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place together.

sections.heading: 2. The electronic concept: loss and gain of electrons
sections.body_md:
In terms of electrons, **oxidation is loss of electrons** and **reduction is gain of electrons**. The electrons lost by one substance are gained by another, so the two changes always go together.

A change is written as a **half-change**, with electrons shown. Atoms and charge must balance, and each electron has a charge of −1.

| Oxidation (electrons on the right) | Reduction (electrons on the left) |
|---|---|
| $\ce{Na -> Na+ + e-}$ | $\ce{Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-}$ |
| $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$ | $\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$ |
| $\ce{Al -> Al^3+ + 3e-}$ | $\ce{Ag+ + e- -> Ag}$ |
| $\ce{Zn -> Zn^2+ + 2e-}$ | $\ce{Pb^2+ + 2e- -> Pb}$ |
| $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$ | $\ce{Fe^3+ + e- -> Fe^2+}$ |
| $\ce{2I- -> I2 + 2e-}$ | $\ce{O + 2e- -> O^2-}$ |

**Sodium and chlorine:** a sodium atom (2, 8, 1) loses its outer electron to become $\ce{Na+}$ (2, 8); a chlorine atom (2, 8, 7) gains one to become $\ce{Cl-}$ (2, 8, 8). Sodium is oxidised; chlorine is reduced.

**Joining two half-changes.** Multiply each half so that the electrons lost equal the electrons gained, then add them; the electrons cancel.
- $\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$ and $\ce{Fe^2+ + 2e- -> Fe}$ give $\ce{Mg + Fe^2+ -> Mg^2+ + Fe}$.
- $2\times(\ce{Al -> Al^3+ + 3e-})$ and $3\times(\ce{Fe^2+ + 2e- -> Fe})$ (six electrons each way) give $\ce{2Al + 3Fe^2+ -> 2Al^3+ + 3Fe}$.

**A metal in a salt solution:** magnesium in blue copper(II) sulphate loses electrons ($\ce{Mg -> Mg^2+ + 2e-}$); copper ions gain them and form reddish-brown copper ($\ce{Cu^2+ + 2e- -> Cu}$).

sections.heading: 3. Oxidising agents, reducing agents and redox reactions
sections.body_md:
| | Oxidising agent | Reducing agent |
|---|---|---|
| Effect on the other substance | Oxidises it | Reduces it |
| What happens to the agent | It is **reduced** | It is **oxidised** |
| Oxygen | Gives oxygen | Removes oxygen |
| Hydrogen | Removes hydrogen | Gives hydrogen |
| Electrons | **Gains** electrons | **Loses** electrons |
| Common examples | Oxygen, chlorine, nitric acid, hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate, potassium dichromate | Hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide, hydrogen sulphide, reactive metals |

**Identifying the agents.** In $\ce{PbO + H2 -> Pb + H2O}$ hydrogen is the reducing agent and lead(II) oxide the oxidising agent. In $\ce{Cl2 + H2S -> 2HCl + S}$ chlorine is the oxidising agent and hydrogen sulphide the reducing agent. In $\ce{Mg + Cu^2+ -> Mg^2+ + Cu}$ magnesium is the reducing agent and the copper(II) ion the oxidising agent.

**Colour changes in redox reactions** (observations): chlorine turns pale green iron(II) chloride solution yellow, $\ce{2FeCl2 + Cl2 -> 2FeCl3}$; chlorine turns colourless potassium iodide solution brown, $\ce{2KI + Cl2 -> 2KCl + I2}$; chlorine and hydrogen sulphide give a yellow deposit of sulphur; lead(II) oxide (yellow) changes to grey lead in hydrogen.

**Not every reaction is redox.** Precipitation ($\ce{AgNO3 + NaCl -> AgCl + NaNO3}$), neutralisation ($\ce{HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O}$) and thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate involve no change of this kind.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that oxidises another substance and is itself reduced; it gains electrons.
A substance that reduces another substance and is itself oxidised; it loses electrons.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that oxidation is the gain of electrons (it is the loss).
- Writing the electrons on the wrong side: oxidation has them on the right, reduction on the left.
- Writing a half-change in which atoms balance but the charge does not.
- Calling the substance that is reduced the reducing agent; the reducing agent is the one that is oxidised.
- Writing ions without the charge, or the charge as a subscript; write Cu²⁺, not Cu₂.
- Naming only the substance oxidised, or only the substance reduced.
- Leaving electrons in a final redox equation, or adding half-changes with unequal numbers of electrons.
- Treating precipitation or neutralisation as redox.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a half-change, an agent, a colour or a name.
- 2 marks: the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, each with a reason; or two half-changes.
- 3 marks: a balanced equation with the agents named.
- 10-mark structured question: a situation or an experiment in parts: observations, equations, half-changes, agents and a count of electrons.

cards.back_md: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place together.

cards.front_md: Why do oxidation and reduction always occur together?
cards.back_md: What one substance loses (oxygen, hydrogen or electrons) another substance gains.

cards.back_md: Loss of electrons.

cards.front_md: Reduction in terms of electrons?
cards.back_md: Gain of electrons.

cards.front_md: Half-change for sodium becoming a sodium ion?
cards.back_md: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation).

cards.front_md: Half-change for chlorine becoming chloride ions?
cards.back_md: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction).

cards.front_md: Half-change for magnesium becoming a magnesium ion?
cards.back_md: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation).

cards.front_md: Half-change for a copper(II) ion becoming copper?
cards.back_md: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction).

cards.front_md: Half-change for Fe²⁺ becoming Fe³⁺?
cards.back_md: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation).

cards.front_md: Where do the electrons appear in an oxidation half-change?
cards.back_md: On the right-hand side.

cards.front_md: Where do the electrons appear in a reduction half-change?
cards.back_md: On the left-hand side.

cards.front_md: What must balance in a half-change?
cards.back_md: Both the atoms and the electric charge.

cards.front_md: Combining Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ with Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Fe?
cards.back_md: Mg + Fe²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Fe; the electrons cancel.

cards.front_md: What is an oxidising agent?
cards.back_md: A substance that oxidises another and is itself reduced; it gains electrons.

cards.front_md: What is a reducing agent?
cards.back_md: A substance that reduces another and is itself oxidised; it loses electrons.

cards.front_md: Three common oxidising agents?
cards.back_md: Oxygen, chlorine, nitric acid (also hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate).

cards.front_md: Four common reducing agents?
cards.back_md: Hydrogen, carbon, carbon monoxide and hydrogen sulphide (also reactive metals).

cards.front_md: In Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu, name the agents.
cards.back_md: Magnesium is the reducing agent; the copper(II) ion is the oxidising agent.

cards.front_md: Colour change when chlorine reacts with iron(II) chloride solution?
cards.back_md: Pale green turns yellow: 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃.

cards.front_md: What is seen when chlorine is passed into potassium iodide solution?
cards.back_md: The solution turns brown as iodine forms.

cards.front_md: Is AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃ a redox reaction?
cards.back_md: No: the ions only swap partners and no electrons are transferred.

questions.solution_md: Two chloride ions are needed for one Cl₂ molecule, and two electrons are lost to balance the charge of −2, option (a).

answer.model_answer_md:

**(e)** To **drive out the air**: a mixture of hydrogen and air **explodes** when it is heated or lit.

questions.stem_md:
Chlorine gas is passed into pale green iron(II) chloride solution until the colour changes to yellow.

(a) Name the product formed and write the balanced equation. [2]

(b) Write the half-change for the oxidation and the half-change for the reduction. [2]

(c) Explain, using electrons, why two iron(II) ions are needed for each chlorine molecule. [2]

(d) Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. [2]

(e) How many chlorine molecules are needed to oxidise 10 iron(II) ions? Show your working. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Iron(III) chloride**: $\ce{2FeCl2 + Cl2 -> 2FeCl3}$

**(b)** Oxidation: $\ce{Fe^2+ -> Fe^3+ + e-}$; reduction: $\ce{Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-}$

**(c)** One chlorine molecule **gains two electrons**, but each iron(II) ion **loses only one**, so **two** iron(II) ions are needed to supply two electrons.

**(d)** Oxidising agent: **chlorine**; reducing agent: **iron(II) chloride** (the iron(II) ion).

**(e)** Two Fe²⁺ ions per Cl₂, so 10 ÷ 2 = **5** molecules.

questions.solution_md: FeCl₃ with equation; two half-changes; two electrons needed; agents; 5 molecules.

marking_scheme.step: One electron lost per iron ion

Chlorine gas is passed into a gas jar containing hydrogen sulphide, and a yellow solid forms on the walls. In another experiment hydrogen sulphide is burnt in a limited supply of air: $\ce{2H2S + O2 -> 2S + 2H2O}$ (the same yellow solid forms).

(a) Name the yellow solid and write the balanced equation for the first experiment. [2]

(b) In the first experiment, name the substance oxidised and the substance reduced, with a reason in terms of hydrogen for each. [2]

(c) Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent in the first experiment. [2]

(d) In the second experiment, name the substance oxidised and the substance reduced. [2]

(e) What is common to hydrogen sulphide in both experiments? [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Sulphur.** $\ce{Cl2 + H2S -> 2HCl + S}$

**(b)** **Hydrogen sulphide** is oxidised because it **loses hydrogen**; **chlorine** is reduced because it **gains hydrogen**.

**(c)** Oxidising agent: **chlorine**; reducing agent: **hydrogen sulphide**.

**(d)** **Hydrogen sulphide** is oxidised; **oxygen** is reduced (it gains hydrogen to form water).

**(e)** In both it **loses hydrogen** to form sulphur, so it is **oxidised** and acts as a **reducing agent**.

questions.stem_md:
A piece of aluminium foil is placed in pale green iron(II) sulphate solution, and grey iron slowly forms. The two half-changes are $\ce{Al -> Al^3+ + 3e-}$ and $\ce{Fe^2+ + 2e- -> Fe}$.

(a) Name the type of change shown by each half-change. [2]

(b) What are the smallest numbers of aluminium atoms and iron(II) ions that make the electrons lost equal to the electrons gained? Show your working. [2]

(c) Write the overall ionic equation, with the electrons cancelled. [3]

(d) Name the oxidising agent and the reducing agent. [2]

(e) How many iron(II) ions are reduced by 4 aluminium atoms? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The aluminium half-change is an **oxidation** (electrons lost); the iron half-change is a **reduction** (electrons gained).

**(b)** Aluminium loses 3 and Fe²⁺ gains 2; the smallest common number is 6. So use **2 aluminium atoms** (2 × 3 = 6) and **3 iron(II) ions** (3 × 2 = 6).

**(c)** $\ce{2Al + 3Fe^2+ -> 2Al^3+ + 3Fe}$

**(d)** Oxidising agent: the **iron(II) ion**; reducing agent: **aluminium**.

**(e)** Two Al reduce three Fe²⁺, so 4 × 3 ÷ 2 = **6** ions.

questions.solution_md: Oxidation and reduction; 2 Al and 3 Fe²⁺ with 6 electrons; overall equation; agents; 6 ions.
